# Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Dermatologic disorders > Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms*

[Original Article Link](/library/bs0Hth)

---

## Summary

Drug reaction with <u>eosinophilia</u> and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome is a rare, potentially life-threatening <u>adverse drug reaction</u> caused by <u>delayed hypersensitivity</u> to medication (most commonly <u>anticonvulsants</u> or antimicrobials). <u>Risk factors</u> include <u>immunosuppression</u>, <u>human herpesvirus-6</u> (<u>HHV-6</u>) infection, and <u>pharmacogenetic susceptibility</u>. DRESS is characterized by delayed onset (2–8 weeks after drug exposure), waxing and waning symptoms, and a prolonged course. Symptoms typically include <u>fever</u>, diffuse <u>rash</u>, facial <u>edema</u>, <u>lymphadenopathy</u>, and internal organ involvement. Peripheral blood <u>eosinophilia</u> is common but not universally observed. Diagnosis is based on medication history, <u>physical exam</u>, blood tests, and <u>skin biopsy</u>. Management typically involves prompt withdrawal of all possible triggering agents, <u>supportive care</u>, and guidance from specialists for any affected organ. Patients should be carefully monitored for internal organ involvement and complications. The <u>liver</u> is the most commonly affected organ, usually with asymptomatic hepatic inflammation; <u>necrosis</u> and <u>liver</u> failure are also possible and the leading <u>cause of death</u> from DRESS.

---

## Etiology

* Common triggers [[2]](/library/ancQ710)[[4]](/library/Yncn710)

* <u>Antiepileptics</u>: <u>lamotrigine</u>, <u>phenytoin</u>, <u>carbamazepine</u>, <u>levetiracetam</u>, <u>phenobarbital</u>

* Antimicrobials: <u>dapsone</u>, <u>sulfamethoxazole</u>/<u>trimethoprim</u>; , <u>piperacillin/tazobactam</u>, <u>vancomycin</u>, <u>minocycline</u>; , <u>abacavir</u>  , <u>nevirapine</u>, <u>sulfonamides</u>

* Other: <u>allopurinol</u>, <u>rifampicin</u>, <u>sulfasalazine</u>

* <u>Risk factors</u>  [[2]](/library/ancQ710)

* <u>Immunosuppression</u>

* <u>Pharmacogenetic susceptibility</u>  [[5]](/library/Tpc6KW0)

---

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of DRESS is not completely understood. Potential mechanisms include: [[2]](/library/ancQ710)




* <u>Delayed hypersensitivity reaction</u> (<u>type IV HSR</u>) to drug metabolites

* Primary infection with or reactivation of <u>HHV-6</u>  [[6]](/library/0nce710)

---

## Clinical features

Clinical manifestations in DRESS have a delayed onset (typically 2–8 weeks) after exposure to the offending agent. In rare cases in which a patient who has recovered from DRESS is reexposed to the triggering agent, the symptom onset is much faster (hours or days).  [[4]](/library/Yncn710)




* Systemic symptoms  [[4]](/library/Yncn710)[[6]](/library/0nce710)

* <u>Fever</u>, typically high (> 38.5Â°C (> 101.3Â°F)) and spiking

* <u>Lymph node</u> enlargement

* <u>Dysphagia</u>

* Diffuse <u>rash</u> 

* Typical manifestation: generalized <u>morbilliform</u> pruritic <u>rash</u> with <u>cephalocaudal</u> progression

* Alternative manifestations: infiltrative <u>papules</u> and <u>plaques</u> with changes that are <u>purpuric</u>, <u>urticarial</u>, lichenoid, <u>pustular</u>, <u>bullous</u>, target-like, or <u>eczematous</u> [[7]](/library/-McDr10)

* Facial <u>edema</u>   [[6]](/library/0nce710)

* Signs of internal organ involvement

* <u>Liver</u> (most common): can be asymptomatic or manifest as <u>hepatomegaly</u> or alterations in <u>liver chemistries</u>

* Renal: decreased <u>GFR</u>, <u>proteinuria</u>, <u>acute interstitial nephritis</u>

* Pulmonary: <u>pneumonitis</u>

* Cardiac and muscle: <u>myocarditis</u>, muscle <u>pain</u>, and/or <u>weakness</u>

* <u>Pancreas</u>: can be asymptomatic elevation in <u>amylase</u> and/or <u>lipase</u>, or <u>pancreatitis</u>

* <u>Multiorgan failure</u> in severe cases





> [!TIP]
> The key features of DRESS are <u>fever</u>, diffuse <u>skin</u> lesions, and symptoms of internal organ involvement. [[2]](/library/ancQ710)[[4]](/library/Yncn710)[[6]](/library/0nce710)




> [!TIP]
> Symptoms in DRESS usually manifest 2–8 weeks after drug exposure and often have a protracted clinical course with waxing and waning of symptoms even after the triggering agent is withdrawn. [[2]](/library/ancQ710)[[4]](/library/Yncn710)[[6]](/library/0nce710)

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[4]](/library/Yncn710)[[7]](/library/-McDr10)




* Consider DRESS in patients with suggestive clinical features (e.g., <u>fever</u>, diffuse <u>rash</u>).

* Obtain a detailed history, with emphasis on the following:

* Medications and supplements started within the last 2–8 weeks

* <u>Family history</u> of drug-induced <u>severe cutaneous adverse reactions</u>

* Obtain <u>laboratory studies</u> and a <u>skin biopsy</u>.

* Assess for internal organ involvement.

* Confirm diagnosis using a validated score (e.g., RegiSCAR).





> [!TIP]
> Early diagnosis is critical to reducing <u>morbidity</u> and mortality, although <u>death</u> can occur even with proper management. [[4]](/library/Yncn710)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[4]](/library/Yncn710)




* Routine <u>laboratory studies</u>

* <u>CBC</u>: <u>eosinophilia</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>, <u>atypical lymphocytes</u> often present

* <u>BMP</u>, <u>liver chemistries</u>, <u>amylase</u>, <u>lipase</u>

* <u>Troponin T</u>, <u>CPK</u>

* <u>Urinalysis</u>

* Exclude alternative diagnoses 

* <u>Serology</u>: <u>viral hepatitis panel</u>, <u>parvovirus B19</u>, <u>HSV</u>–1, <u>HSV</u>–2, <u>chlamydia</u>, <u>mycoplasma</u>

* <u>Blood culture</u>

* <u>Antinuclear antibodies</u>

* Screen for viral reactivation: baseline <u>serology</u> and <u>PCR</u> for <u>HHV</u>–6, <u>HHV</u>–7, <u>CMV</u>, <u>EBV</u>  [[4]](/library/Yncn710)





### <u>Skin biopsy</u> [[4]](/library/Yncn710)[[8]](/library/p7cL5d0)




<u>Biopsy</u> findings in DRESS are typically nonspecific and therefore not required for diagnosis.




* Consider in all patients with suspected DRESS  [[4]](/library/Yncn710)[[8]](/library/p7cL5d0)

* Findings can include:

* <u>Lymphocytic</u> infiltration

* <u>Eosinophils</u>

* <u>Dermal</u> <u>edema</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Biopsy</u> is not required for diagnosis; findings in DRESS are typically nonspecific, so the procedure is most helpful for ruling out other etiologies of <u>rash</u>.




### Evaluation for internal organ involvement [[3]](/library/TIc6Xd0)




The majority of patients (∼ 90%) have involvement of at least one organ/system, most commonly hepatic inflammation. Evaluate all patients for <u>liver</u> and <u>kidney injury</u> and consider other tests depending on the presence of clinical or laboratory features suggestive of involvement of other organs.




* <u>Liver</u> injury  [[4]](/library/Yncn710)

* <u>ALT</u> or <u>conjugated bilirubin</u> ≥ 2 × <u>ULN</u>

* OR <u>AST</u>, total <u>bilirubin</u>, AND <u>alkaline phosphatase</u> all ≥ 2 × <u>ULN</u>

* <u>Acute kidney injury</u> (<u>AKI</u>)

* <u>Creatinine</u> ≥ 1.5 × the base value for the patient

* OR any of the following: ↓ <u>GFR</u>, <u>hematuria</u>, significant <u>proteinuria</u>

* Others

* <u>Myocarditis</u>: Suspect in patients with <u>hypotension</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>chest pain</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>, or <u>palpitations</u>.

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: ↑ <u>CPK</u> and/or ↑ <u>CPK</u>–MB, ↑ <u>troponin</u>

* Other tests: <u>ECG</u> changes , abnormal <u>cardiac imaging</u> (e.g., <u>cMRI</u>), possibly <u>endomyocardial biopsy</u>

* <u>Lung injury</u>: Suspect in patients with <u>cough</u> and/or <u>dyspnea</u>.

* Consider <u>arterial blood gas</u>, <u>bronchoalveolar lavage</u>, or <u>biopsy</u>.

* Imaging may show <u>interstitial</u> involvement.

* <u>Skeletal muscle</u> injury: Suspect in patients with <u>pain</u> or <u>weakness</u>.
* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: ↑ <u>CPK</u> and/or ↑ <u>CPK</u>–MB

* Involvement of the <u>GI tract</u>, <u>pancreas</u>, <u>spleen</u>, <u>CNS</u>, and <u>thyroid gland</u> is also possible.

## Management

### Approach [[4]](/library/Yncn710)




* Stop all suspected offending agents immediately (i.e., <u>drug withdrawal</u>).

* Determine severity based on internal organ involvement [[4]](/library/Yncn710)[[9]](/library/H7cKMd0)

* Nonserious DRESS: No organ involvement, OR <u>AKI stage 1</u>, OR mild <u>liver</u> injury

* Serious DRESS: <u>AKI stage 2</u> and above, OR moderate to severe <u>liver</u> injury , OR involvement of other organs

* Start <u>corticosteroids</u> (topical or systemic based on severity).

* Provide <u>supportive care</u> as needed.

* Post-acute recovery: Consider referral to an allergist  and monitoring for autoimmune sequelae.  [[4]](/library/Yncn710)[[7]](/library/-McDr10)





> [!TIP]
> Withdrawal of all suspected triggering medications is the cornerstone of management for patients with suspected DRESS. Delays in medication withdrawal are associated with a prolonged course and worse prognosis. [[4]](/library/Yncn710)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid empiric NSAIDS and <u>empiric antibiotics</u> (especially <u>amoxicillin</u>) during the acute period as they may prolong or worsen the course. [[4]](/library/Yncn710)




### Nonserious DRESS [[4]](/library/Yncn710)




* Admit all patients with nonserious DRESS to acute care. [[4]](/library/Yncn710)

* Start therapy with <u>topical corticosteroids</u> (high or very high <u>potency</u>, e.g., <u>clobetasol</u> DOSAGE). [[4]](/library/Yncn710)

* Monitor for progression to serious DRESS and escalate therapy if needed. 

* Evaluate for clinical signs and symptoms of organ involvement daily.

* Trend baseline laboratory parameters at least every 72 hours.

* For mild <u>liver</u> injury, reevaluate <u>liver chemistries</u> every 48–72 hours.

* For stage 1 <u>kidney injury</u>, reevaluate <u>kidney function</u> every 48–72 hours.





### Serious DRESS [[4]](/library/Yncn710)




* Admit all patients with serious DRESS.

* Severe organ involvement: Consider <u>ICU</u> admission.

* Severe cutaneous involvement : Consider admission to a <u>burn unit</u>.

* Requires multidisciplinary management; consult specialists for affected organs.

* Perform clinical and laboratory monitoring for new or worsening organ involvement at least every 24 hours.

* Start pharmacological treatment in consultation with a specialist.

* First line: <u>systemic corticosteroids</u> (e.g., <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE) with a prolonged taper  [[4]](/library/Yncn710)

* Refractory cases or contraindications to <u>corticosteroids</u>: Consider <u>cyclosporine</u>, <u>cyclophosphamide</u>, <u>plasmapheresis</u>, or IVIG.  [[6]](/library/0nce710)

* In the case of severe complications of viral reactivation (e.g., <u>HSV encephalitis</u>, <u>CMV colitis</u>): Consider <u>ganciclovir</u> or <u>valganciclovir</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Liver</u> failure secondary to hepatic <u>necrosis</u> is the leading <u>cause of death</u> from DRESS. For patients with severe <u>liver</u> injury, consult hepatology early to evaluate for <u>liver transplant</u> candidacy. [[4]](/library/Yncn710)




### <u>Supportive care</u>




* Start <u>IV fluids</u> and <u>replace electrolytes</u>.

* Consider <u>specialized nutrition support</u> depending on disease severity.

* Consider <u>DVT prophylaxis</u> and <u>gastrointestinal prophylaxis</u>.

* Optimize <u>pain management</u> and use <u>antipyretics</u> as needed.

* Provide <u>skin</u> care and topical treatments.

---

## Prognosis

* DRESS is fatal in ∼10% of cases. [[4]](/library/Yncn710)
